passage:
Monday. In the library, Thomas rolled a small smooth stone between his fingers while Simran quizzed him on circuits for Thursday's viva. "Are you even listening?" she asked, a little sharp. "I am. The stone keeps my head quiet," he said, and answered the next question without a slip.
Thursday. Outside the viva room his palms were damp. He laid both hands flat on the bench, fingers spread wide, and pressed down until his breathing slowed. Inside, he kept the stone in his pocket and touched it once between questions.
Saturday. Simran handed him a new stone she had picked up by the river. "I thought you were bored that day," she admitted. "Turns out you were just holding on." Thomas grinned and said the viva had gone better than any of their mock rounds.

qa.q: When was Thomas's viva?
qa.a: Thomas's viva was on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he pressed his spread fingers on the bench outside the viva room?
qa.a: He was most likely nervous: his palms were damp and he pressed until his breathing slowed. It could partly be habit, but the damp palms before a viva point to nerves.

qa.q: What could Simran do the next time a friend fiddles with something while she talks?
qa.a: She could ask what it does for them before deciding they are bored, since Thomas was answering well the whole time.

qa.q: How did Simran's view of the stone change between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday she read it as not listening and sounded irritated; by Saturday she saw it as the thing that kept Thomas steady and even brought him a new one 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult steadying nerves with a fidget stone and spread fingers, which a friend first mistakes for boredom.

passage: Sit, kanna Kunal. Your cousin says your pen-clicking is rude, so let your Lakshmi Paati tell you something. When I was twenty, I went for my first teaching post interview in Madurai. Five people behind one long table. My hands were shaking so badly I could not hold the tea cup they offered. So I put my hands under the table, pressed my fingers flat and wide against the wood, and pushed. Slowly the shaking went into the table. One man on the panel kept frowning at my arms, as if I were fidgeting and not serious. But the lady at the centre listened to my answers, not my elbows. Months later, after I had joined, she told me she twisted the end of her sari during interviews for the same reason. I got the post, kanna.

qa.q: What could young Lakshmi not hold because her hands were shaking?
qa.a: She could not hold the tea cup they offered.

qa.q: What was young Lakshmi feeling before the interview, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was very anxious: her hands shook so much she could not hold a cup. It could also have been excitement, but the pressing to stop the shaking suggests nerves.

qa.q: What choice did young Lakshmi make when her hands shook, and why did it help?
qa.a: She pressed her spread fingers hard against the table, which let the shaking go into the wood so she could answer steadily.

qa.q: How might the frowning man on the panel have read Lakshmi's arms?
qa.a: He probably took the movement as fidgeting and a sign she was not serious, missing that it was helping her stay calm.

grounding: Shows a young woman quietly pressing spread fingers on a table to calm her nerves while one observer misreads it as unseriousness.

passage: The placement cell's group discussion started forty minutes late, so the panel cut it to ten minutes. A diesel generator droned outside the window. Harish sat with a silver spinner ring on his thumb, turning it round and round under the table. Jomon, the final-year student helping the panel keep notes, wrote "distracted?" beside his name. Then Harish leaned in and summed up the whole argument in three clean points, catching a figure two others had got wrong. After the session Jomon asked him about the ring. "It stops my hands from shaking when I'm put on the spot," Harish said. "Without it I go blank." Jomon looked down at his note, crossed out the word and the question mark, and wrote "clear summariser" instead.

qa.q: How long did the panel cut the group discussion to?
qa.a: The panel cut it to ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Harish's turning of the ring suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Most likely he was nervous about being on the spot, since he says the ring stops his hands shaking. Someone could read it as boredom, but his sharp summary shows he was engaged.

qa.q: What went wrong in Jomon's first note, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Jomon judged the ring as distraction too quickly; looking at what Harish actually said and then asking him about it corrected the note.

qa.q: What would change if Jomon had never asked about the ring?
qa.a: Harish might have been marked as distracted, and a habit that kept him calm could have cost him a fair score.

grounding: Shows a fidget ring helping a nervous candidate stay focused under time pressure, and an observer learning not to read it as disinterest.

passage: I was making tea when Varun called across the flat, "Raghav, is this rude?" He held out his phone. He had sent his internship supervisor a long message about the report delay, ending with a 🙏. The reply was a single thumbs-up, nothing else. Varun paced by the window. "That's a cold thumbs-up. She's annoyed." I honestly couldn't tell. My uncle sends 👍 to everything, even birthday wishes. Varun's friends use it as a polite way of saying "whatever". He typed and deleted three replies. In the end he wrote, "Thanks! Just checking the new date works for you?" Ten minutes later: "Yes, all good, take care 👋". Varun sat down, his shoulders loosening, and I went back to my tea without admitting I'd been worried too.

qa.q: What was the supervisor's reply?
qa.a: The reply was a single thumbs-up, nothing else.

qa.q: Why did Varun pace by the window after the reply came?
qa.a: He was anxious that the lone thumbs-up meant his supervisor was annoyed. It could just as easily have been a quick, neutral okay, which her later warm reply suggests.

qa.q: What small step helped Varun find out what the thumbs-up meant?
qa.a: He sent a friendly follow-up question instead of guessing, which gave the supervisor a chance to answer clearly.

qa.q: How does Raghav see the thumbs-up differently from Varun?
qa.a: Because Raghav's uncle uses it for everything, it can look neutral to Raghav, while Varun's friends use it to mean "whatever".

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a single thumbs-up from an older supervisor as curt, while an onlooker knows the same emoji means different things in different circles.

passage:
Monday. Kalyani texted, "Posters are up 👍". Pallavi, who ran the college blood-donation drive, replied with a single 🙏. Kalyani frowned at it. Among her friends that meant "please, please", so was she being asked for more?
Wednesday. Kalyani stayed back to count forms, and another folded-hands arrived. At the stall she had seen Pallavi press her palms together to every volunteer while saying "thank you, beta", and she began to wonder if the message meant the same.
Saturday. As they packed up after the drive, Pallavi laughed. "You young people send that thumb and I think you are cross with me!" Kalyani laughed too. "And I thought your folded hands meant you wanted more work." From then on Kalyani typed "Thank you, ma'am 🙂" and Pallavi kept her folded hands.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do on Wednesday after the drive work?
qa.a: She stayed back to count forms.

qa.q: What was Kalyani worried about when she first saw the folded-hands emoji?
qa.a: She was uneasy that it meant "please, please" and that more work was being asked of her; the other reading, a thank-you, turned out to be what Pallavi meant.

qa.q: What helped Kalyani read the emoji better?
qa.a: She compared it with how Pallavi pressed her palms together in person and then talked about it openly, instead of relying only on her friends' habits.

qa.q: How did Pallavi read Kalyani's thumbs-up?
qa.a: Pallavi took the thumb as a sign the young volunteers were cross with her, which shows the same emoji can land differently across ages 😅

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that folded-hands and thumbs-up emoji carry different meanings for an older coordinator than for friends her own age.

passage: You're asking whether a thumbs-up is rude, Lavanya? The juniors here still call me Nilesh sir, but at twenty-two I nearly lost a mentor over one. I was a trainee at an architecture firm. Mrs Kamath, our senior partner, sent me four paragraphs of careful notes on my first drawing. I was on a site in the rain, so I replied with a thumbs-up and nothing else. Next morning she was cool with me, and she passed my file to someone else. I sulked for a whole day. Then I went to her cabin and asked what I had done. "I wrote you a page," she said, "and you sent me a thumb." To me it had meant "got it, thank you". To her it meant I had not bothered. After that I wrote one real line back, even from a muddy site.

qa.q: Where was young Nilesh when he replied with the thumbs-up?
qa.a: He was on a site in the rain.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when his file was passed to someone else?
qa.a: He felt hurt and sulked for a whole day; he was probably also confused, because to him the thumbs-up had only meant "got it, thank you".

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Nilesh repair things with Mrs Kamath?
qa.a: Going to her cabin and asking what he had done, instead of sulking longer, let her explain how the thumb had felt to her.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kamath see the lone thumbs-up?
qa.a: After writing a page of careful notes, she saw the single thumb as a sign that he had not bothered, even though he meant thanks.

grounding: Shows how a thumbs-up meant as thanks by a young trainee read as curt to an older senior, and how asking cleared it up.

passage:
First evening in São Paulo. Ganga made a circle with her thumb and finger to tell the waiter the food was perfect. His smile froze for half a second before he moved on. Ishita, across the table, raised her eyebrows but said nothing.
Next morning Ganga asked the hostel receptionist, trying not to sound silly. The receptionist winced kindly. "For many people here that sign is rude. Young people might just laugh, but my grandmother would be shocked." Ganga covered her face, cheeks hot.
Four days later, at a fruit market, a vendor handed her a mango slice to taste. Ganga's hand started to lift into the circle, then stopped. She smiled, put a palm to her chest and said, "Obrigada, delicious!" The vendor beamed. Ishita nudged her. "Learning fast."

qa.q: What did Ganga put to her chest at the fruit market?
qa.a: She put a palm to her chest.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she covered her face at the hostel?
qa.a: She was embarrassed, with hot cheeks, on learning the circle sign could be rude; she may also have felt relieved that the waiter had only frozen for a moment.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Ganga at the market, and why?
qa.a: Stopping the circle sign and using a smile, a hand on her chest and a spoken thanks worked, because those carry no rude meaning there.

qa.q: What might the waiter have thought when Ganga made the circle sign?
qa.a: He may have taken it as rude, or he may have guessed she was a tourist meaning praise; his brief frozen smile leaves both possible.

grounding: Shows a young traveller finding that the OK-sign can offend abroad and switching to a smile and spoken thanks.

passage: Bidisha, before you pack your bag, listen to your Sarika Masi's story. At twenty I went on a college exchange to a small town in Greece. On my second day I missed the bus stop, so I stood by the road and held up my thumb to ask the next bus to wait. An old man on a bench scowled and muttered at me. I thought he was just a grumpy uncle. That evening my host, Eleni, laughed and then turned serious. "Some older people here take that thumb as an insult," she said. I felt my ears burn. I had been so proud of being friendly! After that, whenever I was unsure, I did what I did at home: palms together, a small nod, a smile. Nobody ever scowled at that. The old man on the bench even nodded back the next week.

qa.q: What did young Sarika hold up to ask the bus to wait?
qa.a: She held up her thumb.

qa.q: How did young Sarika feel when Eleni explained the thumb sign?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her ears burning, because she had been proud of being friendly; she may also have felt grateful to learn it early.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Sarika greeted people?
qa.a: After Eleni's explanation, she chose palms together, a small nod and a smile whenever she was unsure, and nobody took offence.

qa.q: How might the old man on the bench have seen young Sarika's thumb?
qa.a: He may have taken the thumb as a rude sign from a stranger, which is why he scowled; later her folded hands and nod felt respectful enough that he nodded back.

grounding: Shows a young traveller discovering that a thumbs-up can be offensive in another country and turning to a neutral greeting.

passage: The last bus had gone, Vishal's phone was dead, and the hill-town station was packed with families shouting over the loudspeaker. Jaya knew about twelve words of the language. At the ticket window, the clerk listened to her halting question, tilted his head sideways twice and pointed to platform three. Jaya couldn't tell if the tilt meant yes, no or "maybe". She almost made the circle sign with her fingers to say "okay?", then remembered their host warning them it was rude here. Instead she held up the paper with the town's name, pointed at it, then at platform three, and raised her eyebrows. The clerk nodded firmly and wrote "21:40" on the paper. Jaya put her palms together and said one of her twelve words, "thank you". The clerk smiled. Vishal let out a breath.

qa.q: Which platform did the clerk point to?
qa.a: The clerk pointed to platform three.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she could not read the clerk's head tilt?
qa.a: She was unsure and probably anxious, with no phone and the last bus gone; the tilt could have meant yes, no or maybe, so she did not trust her own guess.

qa.q: What could Jaya try next time she is unsure what a gesture means abroad?
qa.a: She could do what worked here: skip risky hand signs, point to written words and use a simple spoken thanks with a neutral gesture.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had made the circle sign at the window?
qa.a: The clerk might have felt insulted, and with the station crowded and time short, a stranded pair could have lost the one person helping them.

grounding: Shows a young traveller under pressure avoiding a hand sign that is rude locally and using writing, pointing and a neutral greeting instead.

passage: I'm Jyoti, and I was sitting opposite Vishal in our university canteen in Manila, three weeks into the exchange. He wanted more water, so he lifted his hand, palm up, and curled one finger at the server. She came, but her face had gone flat, and she set the jug down harder than needed. Vishal didn't seem to notice, or maybe he did; he rubbed the back of his neck afterwards. Our classmate Marites leaned over and said quietly that many people here use that sign only for dogs. Vishal went red. Marites showed us how she calls someone: palm down, fingers scooping towards herself, exactly like my grandmother does back home. The next day I saw Vishal raise his hand, palm down, scoop gently and smile at the same server. She smiled back.

qa.q: How did Marites show she calls someone?
qa.a: Palm down, fingers scooping towards herself.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when Marites explained the sign?
qa.a: He went red, which suggests he felt embarrassed; rubbing his neck earlier may mean he already sensed something was off, or it may have been nothing.

qa.q: What did Vishal do well the next day?
qa.a: He used the palm-down scoop Marites showed and added a smile, which showed respect for how people there call someone.

qa.q: How did the server seem to see Vishal's finger beckon?
qa.a: Her flat face and the jug set down hard suggest she felt treated rudely, as if called like a dog.

grounding: Shows a student abroad learning that the upturned-finger beckon is rude there and that the palm-down scoop is the local way.

passage:
Day one. In the university library in Melbourne, Seema spotted Emma from her tutorial group and called her over the way she would at home: palm down, fingers scooping. Emma gave a small awkward smile and walked the other way. Seema sat very still, wondering what she had done.
Day three. Over chai in the hostel kitchen, Seema told Karthik, who had studied there for three years. He laughed gently. "Here that can look like 'go away'. Most people wave with the palm up or just say your name." Then he added, "Or maybe she was late for class. Don't decide yet."
Day six. Seema saw Emma across the quad, waved high and called, "Emma, over here!" Emma jogged across. When Seema explained, Emma groaned. "I thought you were shooing me off! I felt so rude walking away."

qa.q: What did Karthik say most people there do instead of the scoop?
qa.a: Most people wave with the palm up or just say your name.

qa.q: How was Seema feeling after Emma walked away on day one?
qa.a: She was confused and a little hurt, sitting very still and wondering what she had done; she could not yet tell whether Emma was offended or just busy.

qa.q: What made Karthik's advice wise?
qa.a: He explained the local meaning but also warned Seema not to decide yet, which kept her from assuming Emma disliked her.

qa.q: What was it like for Emma when Seema made the palm-down gesture?
qa.a: Emma thought she was being shooed away, felt awkward, and later felt bad about walking off.

grounding: Shows a student abroad finding that a palm-down beckon friendly at home can read as 'go away' elsewhere, and learning by asking.

passage: Bhavna beti, you leave for your course next month, so let your old Rafiq Chacha tell you about my first ship. I was twenty-one, a trainee engineer, and the captain was a tall Norwegian named Mr Hagen. One morning in the engine room I needed him to look at a leaking valve. I called him the way my mother called me at home: hand out, palm down, fingers scooping. He looked at me, nodded, and walked away up the ladder. I stood there fuming, thinking he did not care about my valve. At lunch the cook, who had sailed with many crews, told me that for the captain my scoop looked like 'go on, off you go'. So that evening I went up, said his name clearly and asked him to come. He came at once. After that, in every new port, I watched how the dockworkers called each other before I ever lifted a hand.

qa.q: What did young Rafiq need the captain to look at?
qa.a: He needed him to look at a leaking valve.

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when the captain walked away up the ladder?
qa.a: He was angry, standing there fuming, because he thought the captain did not care about the valve; in fact it was a misreading of his gesture.

qa.q: What choice in the story fixed the problem with the captain?
qa.a: Rafiq went up, said the captain's name clearly and asked him to come, using words instead of a gesture that meant something else to him.

qa.q: How did Mr Hagen likely see Rafiq's palm-down scoop?
qa.a: He probably read it as being sent off, so he nodded and left, not realising Rafiq was calling him closer.

grounding: Shows a young trainee learning that a palm-down beckon can read as 'go away' to someone from another culture, and that watching locals and asking works better.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage:
Kishore: seminar was a disaster. I had a point on the water data and never got in 😔
Shalini: I saw you lean forward twice. Why didn't you just jump in like Deepak?
Kishore: Deepak cut Ma'am off mid-sentence. She looked annoyed
Shalini: true 😅 she made him wait after that
Kishore: I lifted one finger. Maybe nobody saw
Shalini: I saw it! Ma'am did too I think, she nodded at you right before time ran out
Kishore: I thought that nod meant "not now"
Shalini: could be either tbh. Next week sit where she can see your face and catch her eye when someone is finishing
Kishore: and if she still doesn't call me?
Shalini: say "May I add something?" in the pause. Polite, not a grab 👍
Kishore: ok. trying it Thursday. Deepak can keep interrupting

qa.q: What was Kishore's point about?
qa.a: His point was on the water data.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling after the seminar?
qa.a: He was disappointed and frustrated that his point never got in; he may also have felt unsure, since he read Ma'am's nod as "not now" when it may have been a sign she had seen him.

qa.q: What small steps does Shalini suggest to help Kishore get a turn?
qa.a: Sit where the chair can see his face, catch her eye as someone finishes, and ask "May I add something?" in a pause.

qa.q: How might Ma'am have seen Deepak's interruption compared with Kishore's lifted finger?
qa.a: She seemed annoyed at Deepak for cutting her off, while Kishore's quiet finger showed he wanted a turn without grabbing it, which she may have respected.

grounding: Shows a young adult signalling for a turn with a lifted finger and leaning in, and contrasts this with interrupting.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: The ceiling fan in the Kalimpong college seminar room creaked with every turn. Aparna Ma'am had asked the second-years whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat. Dolma had a point about the vegetable sellers from her village, who had no other bags. She lifted one finger just above the desk and leaned a little forward. Bikash, beside her, thought she was stretching. Then Suraj started speaking over the girl who was already talking. Dolma kept her finger up and watched Aparna Ma'am's face. When Suraj finally paused, Ma'am turned. "Dolma, you've been waiting. Go on." Dolma spoke slowly about the sellers and the bags. Two students wrote it down, and Ma'am said, "That changes the question." Bikash whispered, "I thought you were just yawning."

qa.q: What was the seminar question about?
qa.a: Whether the town should ban plastic at the weekly haat.

qa.q: What does Dolma's lifted finger and forward lean suggest about her?
qa.a: They suggest she was eager to contribute and determined to wait her turn; Bikash read the same movement as stretching, which shows these cues can be missed.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, Suraj's or Dolma's, and why?
qa.a: Dolma's, because she signalled and waited, so when Aparna Ma'am called on her the room listened and wrote down her point.

qa.q: How did Bikash see Dolma's signal?
qa.a: He thought she was stretching or yawning, so he did not realise she had something to say until Ma'am called on her.

grounding: Shows a student using a lifted finger, a lean and eye contact with the chair to claim a turn, and how patient signalling earns a hearing.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: At home in Bogotá, Camila's family talked over each other at dinner and nobody minded. In her first seminar in Prague she jumped in twice while others were mid-sentence, and she saw two classmates exchange a glance. Maybe it was about her, maybe not, but her face went warm. The next week she tried something else. She held her pen upright just above her notes, leaned forward slightly and looked at Jana, the tutor, each time a speaker slowed down. For a few minutes nothing happened, and Camila's jaw tightened. Then Jana met her eyes and gave a small nod. "Camila, go ahead." Camila explained her idea about the housing survey, and one of the classmates who had glanced at her the week before asked her a follow-up question. After class Jana said, "I saw you waiting. Keep doing that."

qa.q: Where did Camila's first seminar take place?
qa.a: In Prague.

qa.q: How did Camila feel when she saw two classmates exchange a glance?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face going warm, worried the glance was about her interrupting; it may also have been about something else entirely.

qa.q: What could Camila keep doing in future seminars?
qa.a: Keep signalling with a raised pen, a slight lean and eye contact with the chair, and wait to be invited in instead of cutting in.

qa.q: What was it like for Jana to see Camila signal instead of interrupting?
qa.a: Jana noticed her waiting and appreciated it enough to encourage her, which made it easier to give her a turn.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to replace interrupting with a raised pen, a lean and eye contact to claim a turn in a seminar.

passage:
Dear Harish,
You asked how the thesis presentation went. Better than the rehearsal, and I owe that to the video you told me to take.
When I watched it on Sunday I nearly deleted it. My arms were windmilling on every sentence. At one point I flung my hand so wide I knocked the pointer off the table. You could not look at the slides for all the waving.
So I planned my gestures like slides. For the rise in the rainfall graph, one flat hand climbing slowly. For the three stages of the filter, three fingers, one at a time. Everything else, hands resting loosely on the lectern.
On Tuesday Professor Roy followed the graph with her eyes when my hand rose, and nodded. My hands still twitched once or twice, but it felt like they were helping.
Thanks for the push,
Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila knock off the table in the rehearsal video?
qa.a: The pointer.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when first watching the rehearsal video?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed enough to nearly delete it, seeing the windmilling arms; there is also some relief later, as the video showed exactly what to change.

qa.q: What went wrong in the rehearsal, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Large, constant arm movements pulled attention away from the slides; planning a few purposeful gestures and resting the hands otherwise fixed it.

qa.q: How does Professor Roy seem to experience the final presentation?
qa.a: She follows the graph with her eyes as Sharmila's hand rises and nods, so the gesture helped her understand instead of distracting her.

grounding: Shows a young adult trimming over-large gestures after watching a rehearsal video and using purposeful hand shapes to show a graph and a process.

passage: Nikita, you know me, Kalyani, the girl who talks with her whole body. So picture my final-year presentation on the metro line plan. I was so nervous I was waving both hands like I was directing traffic. And I noticed Dr Menon wasn't looking at my slides at all. His eyes kept following my hands, left, right, up. Awful. That night I propped my phone on a stack of books and recorded myself. Honestly, watching it, I cringed. There was one good gesture, though. When I said the line would curve round the lake, my hand drew the curve slowly, and it actually made sense. So I kept that, and one for 'three stations', and I made myself rest my hands on the table for the rest. At the second round, Dr Menon asked a question about the lake curve. He'd been following.

qa.q: Where did Kalyani prop the phone to record herself?
qa.a: On a stack of books.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she noticed Dr Menon's eyes following her hands?
qa.a: She felt awful and embarrassed, seeing he was watching her hands instead of her slides; the waving itself also suggests she was nervous.

qa.q: What could someone like Kalyani try before a big presentation?
qa.a: Record a rehearsal, keep the gestures that clearly show an idea, like drawing a curve, and rest the hands the rest of the time.

qa.q: What was it like for Dr Menon during the first round?
qa.a: He seemed pulled away from the slides because his eyes kept following her hands; by the second round he was following the content well enough to ask about the curve.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing that busy gestures distract a listener and keeping only purposeful ones after recording a rehearsal.

passage: I'm Nirmala, and I sat in the second row for Chetan's lab presentation on water recycling. He's usually quiet, so I watched him closely. His first two minutes were rough: he kept jingling his keys in one pocket, and the girl next to me started tapping her pen to the same rhythm. I couldn't tell if he was nervous or just used to it. Then he reached the recycling loop. He drew a slow circle in the air with one hand and stopped at four points around it, naming each stage. Suddenly the whole room was looking where his hand was. After that his hand stayed out of his pocket. Later I asked if he'd practised. He shrugged and said he'd filmed himself twice and cut out "the key thing". Whether he felt calm by the end, I don't know, but he looked it.

qa.q: What did Chetan keep jingling in his pocket?
qa.a: His keys.

qa.q: What might Chetan have been feeling during the first two minutes?
qa.a: He may have been nervous, which the key-jingling suggests; Nirmala notes it could also just be a habit, so she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What small step had helped Chetan improve his gestures?
qa.a: Filming himself twice, which let him cut the key jingling and keep a clear circle gesture for the recycling loop.

qa.q: How did the audience experience the circle gesture compared with the jingling keys?
qa.a: The jingling pulled attention away and even set a pen tapping, while the circle made the whole room look where his hand was and follow the loop.

grounding: Shows through an observer how purposeful gestures help listeners follow a process while fidgety movements distract.

passage: The college fest stage was blasting music so loud that Akash could not hear his own voice. He had finally met Uday, the Deaf student from the photography club, and they had only ten minutes before Uday's bus. Akash tried to ask where Uday lived by miming a house and pointing, eyebrows flat, arms flapping. Uday smiled, then signed something with his eyebrows raised high and his head pushed slightly forward. His friend Nisha typed on her phone for Akash: "He's asking you a question. The eyebrows make it one." Akash stared. The raised eyebrows did the job his voice would have done. Around them, hearing people were shouting and failing, while Uday and Nisha kept signing easily across the noise. Before the bus came, Akash typed, "Can you teach me a few signs properly?" Uday nodded and signed a reply, and Nisha typed: "Saturday, library."

qa.q: How long did Akash and Uday have before Uday's bus?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Nisha explained Uday's raised eyebrows?
qa.a: He was surprised and curious, staring as he realised the eyebrows did the work of his voice; he may also have felt a little silly about his flapping mime.

qa.q: What was a respectful step Akash took before the bus came?
qa.a: He asked Uday to teach him a few signs properly, which treated signing as a language to learn rather than something to guess at.

qa.q: What might it be like for Uday when Akash mimes with flapping arms?
qa.a: Uday smiles, so he may find it friendly but also a sign that Akash sees signing as acting out, not a language with its own grammar.

grounding: Shows a student discovering that facial grammar and structure make sign language a full language, not mime, in a noisy setting.

passage: Wasim was the only hearing person at Tanvir's birthday dinner in a Pune café. Tanvir's Deaf friends signed fast across the table, laughing, and Wasim tried to join in by waving his hands and pulling faces, the way he might play charades. Tanvir's sister Farah watched him, amused but tired. Then Wasim noticed something. When Farah told a story about two friends, she set one to her left and one to her right in the air, and later just pointed back to those spots instead of repeating them. Her face changed with every line. It was like watching someone keep a map as they spoke. Wasim put his hands down. He typed on his phone and turned it to Tanvir: "I've been acting things out. That's not how it works, is it? Can you show me how to say happy birthday properly?" Tanvir grinned and taught him.

qa.a: In a Pune café.

grounding: Shows a hearing young adult realising sign language uses space and facial grammar as a full language and asking to learn.

passage:
"Okay, so sign language is basically miming, right?" Nilesh asked as they queued for coffee.
Maria put down her cup. "Where did that come from?"
"Your cousin Joel at the party. I tried acting out 'Do you want food?' and he looked at me like I was a toddler."
Maria laughed. "Joel's Deaf, not bored. He's got a whole language. Handshape, movement, where the sign is made, his face. Change one and it's a different word."
"Even the face?"
"Especially the face. His eyebrows can turn a sentence into a question."
Nilesh groaned. "So I was doing baby charades at him."
"A bit." Maria softened. "He'd rather you try. Just try properly. Ask him to teach you the greeting, and learn the alphabet to spell your name."
"Would he mind me asking?"
"He'd mind you guessing more."

qa.q: Where did Nilesh meet Maria's cousin Joel?
qa.a: At the party.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel when he realises what his miming looked like?
qa.a: He groans, which suggests he feels embarrassed about doing "baby charades"; he also seems eager, asking whether Joel would mind being asked.

qa.q: What would you advise Nilesh before he meets Joel again?
qa.a: Follow Maria's advice: ask Joel to teach him the greeting and learn the alphabet to spell his name, instead of guessing with mime.

qa.q: How might Joel have felt when Nilesh acted out food?
qa.a: He may have felt talked down to, like being treated as a toddler, since Nilesh treated his language as loose miming.

grounding: Shows a student learning from a friend that a sign language is a complete language with its own grammar and that asking respectfully builds connection.

passage: Anjali came home to the village for the Diwali break full of news about her college in the city. passage: In their tiny Lisbon flat, Gabriel spread his sketches on the floor and pitched the idea: a street band playing every Sunday by the river. Pablo leaned right in, elbows on knees, asking which songs. Gabriel's hopes rose. Then, halfway through the plan for rehearsals, Pablo sat back on the sofa, looked at the ceiling and went quiet. Gabriel's stomach dropped. He rolled up the sketches. "Forget it, it's a silly idea." Pablo blinked. "What? No, wait. I was imagining the trumpet part. I lean back when I'm hearing music in my head." Gabriel unrolled the paper slowly. "I thought you'd lost interest." "I was more interested, not less," Pablo said. "Also, is Sunday morning realistic? We're never awake." They both laughed, and Gabriel crossed out "Sunday morning" and wrote "Sunday evening".

qa.q: Where did Gabriel want the band to play?
qa.a: By the river.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling when Pablo sat back and went quiet?
qa.a: He was disappointed, his stomach dropping, because he read the lean back as lost interest; in fact Pablo was imagining the trumpet part.

qa.q: What could Gabriel try next time a listener leans back?
qa.a: Ask what they are thinking before giving up on the idea, since leaning back is only a weak cue.

qa.q: How did Pablo experience Gabriel rolling up the sketches?
qa.a: He was surprised and confused, because he felt more interested, not less, and had to explain quickly to stop the idea being dropped.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading a friend's lean back as distance when it meant absorption, and how checking fixed it.

passage: The district entrance exam was held in the government school in Sirsa, with desks too small and a single fan. Wasim turned the paper over, read the first physics question and felt his whole body lock. His shoulders rose to his ears. He realised he had not breathed out for a while. His friend Varun, two rows ahead, glanced back and saw Wasim hunched over the desk like a closed fist. Wasim remembered what his coaching sir had drilled into them: breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in; drop your shoulders; feel both feet on the floor. He did it three times. His shoulders came down. The question was still hard, so he skipped it and did the next one. Outside afterwards Varun said, "You looked frozen at the start." Wasim nodded. "I was. Then I wasn't."

qa.q: Where was the district entrance exam held?
qa.a: In the government school in Sirsa.

qa.q: What does Wasim's hunching and held breath suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests a spike of anxiety at the hard first question; it could also be deep concentration, but his later relief once his shoulders dropped points to fear.

qa.q: Which steps helped Wasim unfreeze, and why?
qa.a: Slow exhaling, dropping his shoulders and feeling his feet on the floor calmed his body enough that he could think and move on.

qa.q: How did Varun see Wasim at the start of the exam?
qa.a: Varun saw him hunched like a closed fist and thought he looked frozen, though from two rows ahead he could not know exactly what Wasim felt.

grounding: Shows a young adult stiffening and holding the breath under exam stress and easing it with slow exhales, dropped shoulders and grounded feet.

passage: It was Javier's third week at a noodle bar in Osaka. A customer at the counter slapped the menu down and began shouting that his order was wrong. Javier's Japanese was still slow, and his body went rigid. His hands froze on the tray; he could not tell if he had breathed in the last few seconds. Kaito, the senior cook, glanced over from the pot. He did not step in. He just let out one long, obvious breath and rolled his shoulders down, catching Javier's eye. Javier copied him. Out went the breath. Down went his shoulders. He pressed his heels into the floor. His voice came back. "Sorry. Let me check," he said, and read the order slip. It was the right dish, but he offered to call the manager. The man grumbled and sat. Later Kaito only said, "Breathe first, then talk."

qa.q: Where was Javier working?
qa.a: At a noodle bar in Osaka.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling when the customer started shouting?
qa.a: He was frightened and anxious, his body going rigid and his hands freezing on the tray; being new and still slow at the language made it worse.

qa.q: How did Kaito support Javier without taking over?
qa.a: He modelled a long exhale and dropped shoulders and caught Javier's eye, letting Javier calm himself and handle the customer.

qa.q: How might Kaito have seen Javier freezing?
qa.a: He likely recognised the freeze as stress rather than rudeness, which is why he responded with a calming breath instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a young worker stiffening in a confrontation and easing the freeze through slow exhaling, dropping the shoulders and grounding the feet.

passage: The hostel committee had called Nirmala to the warden's office after her roommate complained about late-night noise. Warden Baljeet Kaur sat behind a steel desk with the complaint in front of her. As she read it aloud, Nirmala hunched in the chair, arms pinned to her sides, jaw tight. She could not get a word out. Mrs Kaur paused. "You seem very tense. Are you refusing to speak?" Nirmala shook her head. She remembered the counsellor's workshop: breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, press the feet down. She did it twice while the warden waited. Her arms loosened. "I'm not refusing, ma'am. I just froze," she said. Then she explained that the noise had been a video call with her mother in the hospital. Mrs Kaur's face softened. "Next time, tell your roommate. And come to me."

qa.q: Why had Nirmala been called to the warden's office?
qa.a: Her roommate had complained about late-night noise.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's hunching and tight jaw suggest?
qa.a: They suggest fear and anxiety at being called in; Mrs Kaur briefly read them as refusing to speak, which shows the same stiffness can be misread as defiance.

qa.q: What small step helped Nirmala explain herself?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly, letting her shoulders fall and pressing her feet down loosened her enough to speak.

qa.q: How did the warden's view change during the meeting?
qa.a: Mrs Kaur first wondered if Nirmala was refusing to speak, then softened once she understood the freeze and heard about the call.

grounding: Shows a young adult freezing and hunching in a stressful confrontation and using slow breathing and grounding to recover.
